Q098.L1t: A truth table for an argument with three sentence letters has eight rows, one for each combination of truth values.
Q098.L2t: An argument is invalid exactly when some row makes every premise true and the conclusion false.
Q098.L3t: The second premise, a conjunction with a negated S, is true only when S is false and U is true, so only rows with those values can make all the premises true; check whether the conclusion fails in them.
Q098.L4t: The argument is invalid, because the row with S false, T false and U true makes all three premises true while the conclusion is false.
Q098.L2f: A truth table for three sentence letters needs only four rows, because the values of the third letter are fixed by the other two.
Q098.L3f: A negated letter is true when the letter itself is true, so the second premise is satisfied in rows where S and U are both true.
Q098.L4f: The argument is invalid, and the row with S and U true and T false is a counterexample.

Q099.L1t: Predicate logic translates English statements using quantifiers, predicate letters and truth-functional connectives.
Q099.L2t: In this translation R and A stand for the properties 'is a robot' and 'is an artifact', and the universal quantifier ranges over everything in the domain.
Q099.L3t: The sentence says that for anything at all, if it is a robot then it is an artifact, and it says nothing about non-robots, so a universal claim about a restricted class needs a conditional.
Q099.L4t: The sentence is correctly rendered as a universally quantified conditional with robot as the antecedent and artifact as the consequent.
Q099.L2f: In translations like this, predicate letters name particular individuals rather than standing for properties.
Q099.L3f: A universal claim says that everything in the domain has both properties, so the two predicates should be joined by conjunction under the quantifier.
Q099.L4f: The correct translation is the universally quantified conjunction of robot and artifact.

Q110.L1t: The free-electron model explains many of the electrical and thermal properties of metals.
Q110.L2t: Conduction electrons in a typical metal have Fermi energies of several electron volts, while kT at room temperature is only about 0.025 eV.
Q110.L3t: The Pauli exclusion principle allows at most one electron per quantum state, so filling states from the bottom up forces most electrons into high-energy states even at very low temperature.
Q110.L4t: Exclusion forces the electrons to fill states up to a high Fermi energy, forming a degenerate Fermi gas, so their mean kinetic energy far exceeds kT.
Q110.L2f: At room temperature the electronic heat capacity of a metal is roughly the classical value of 3/2 k per electron.
Q110.L3f: Conduction electrons in metals travel at speeds close to the speed of light, so relativistic kinetic energy dominates their motion.
Q110.L4f: Electrons in metals are highly relativistic, which is why their mean kinetic energy greatly exceeds kT.
